title: Rights and responsibilities
blurb: What you can expect from the CRA, and what it expects from you.

levels.title: Your rights
learn: Say how many rights the Taxpayer Bill of Rights lists.
Match a made-up situation to the one right that fits it.

cards.text: The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) has a Taxpayer Bill of Rights. It lists 16 rights that describe how you are entitled to be treated when you deal with the CRA. You do not need to memorise them. Here are the ideas behind a few.

image.alt: An open blank booklet with a ribbon on a desk

cards.text: Some rights are about money. You have the right to "receive entitlements and pay no more and no less than required by law". An entitlement is something the law says you are owed, such as a refund. You also have the right to "relief from penalties and interest because of extraordinary circumstances".

image.alt: A balance scale with gold discs and a blank sheet

cards.text: Some rights are about information. You have the right to "service in both official languages", which means English or French. You have the right to "privacy and confidentiality". And you have the right to "complete, accurate, clear, and timely information".

image.alt: A blank envelope with a padlock beside folders

cards.text: Some rights are about disagreeing. You have the right to "a formal review and a subsequent appeal", and to "be represented by a person of your choice". You can "lodge a service complaint and request a formal review without fear of reprisal". Reprisal means being punished for it.

image.alt: Two empty chairs across a desk with a blank sheet

cards.text: Some rights are about fair treatment. You have the right to "be treated professionally, courteously, and fairly" and to "have the law applied consistently". Unless the law says otherwise, you have the right "not to pay income tax amounts in dispute before an impartial review". Impartial means fair.

image.alt: A wooden bench with a blank clipboard in a hallway

That right is about keeping your information private, not about paying a disputed amount.

options.why: That right is about keeping your information private, not about how a rule is applied.
That right is about English or French, not about how a rule is applied.
You have the right to have the law applied consistently, the same way for everyone.

options.text: be represented by a person of your choice

levels.title: Your responsibilities
learn: Name what the CRA expects you to do, and when.
Use the dates and the late balance rule on made-up people.

cards.text: Rights come with responsibilities. A responsibility is something you are expected to do. Here are five, and the next cards take them in turn: doing your taxes by the deadline, giving accurate and complete information, paying your balance owing, correcting your taxes, updating your personal information.

image.alt: Three plain books with a brass key on a desk

cards.text: Most people must file by April 30 of the year after the tax year, so for the 2025 return that is April 30, 2026. If you or your spouse or common-law partner is self-employed, the filing deadline is June 15. Here are the dates for the 2025 return.

Giving accurate and complete information means giving the CRA what it needs to process your return correctly. Your slips show the income you were paid and the tax and other amounts taken off. Gather your slips, such as T4s, and your receipts.

image.alt: A stack of blank slips and receipts with a clip

cards.text: A balance owing is the tax you still owe when you do your taxes. It is also due on April 30. If you do not pay it by then, the CRA starts charging compound daily interest as of May 1. Compound means interest is charged on the interest already added.

image.alt: A blank calendar page beside a jar of gold discs

cards.text: If you make a mistake on your return, or leave out details about your income, you have the chance to correct it. If your personal information changes, like your address, you should update it with the CRA.

image.alt: A blank form with a pencil and eraser by a mailbox
